title: Case Reading and Legal Reasoning
description: Read judicial opinions with attention to procedural posture, identify holdings and reasoning, synthesize rules across cases, and analyze changed facts. Second course in the J.D. Preparation pathway; includes an original three-opinion practice packet.
author: Erudior
disclaimer: Independent educational preparation only; not legal advice, university credit, a J.D. degree, or a determination of bar eligibility. Alder law and opinions are fictional teaching materials. Research current jurisdiction-specific law for real matters.

modules.title: Reading an opinion and procedural posture

lessons.title: Finding your way through a judicial opinion
lessons.body:
## Start with a question, not a highlighter

Introduction to the U.S. Legal System introduced courts and authority. This course
changes the task: you will read what a court actually decided, explain how it got
there, and use that reasoning on a different problem. By the end of this lesson,
you should be able to make an opinion map that separates the court's work from
the parties' stories. Keep the Alder practice packet open beside you. All its law,
judges and cases are original fiction for learning; they are not legal authority.

A judicial **[[opinion]]** explains a court's decision and reasoning. It is not a neutral
encyclopedia entry about every possible rule. The writer selects facts and arguments
relevant to a particular dispute at a particular stage. Your first question is therefore
not “What is the law about equipment?” It is “What was this court being asked to do?”
That question keeps a narrow ruling from becoming an invented universal rule.

The **[[caption]]** identifies the case and its parties. It is a useful starting point,
but does not alone tell you who is appealing or which party won below. A **[[citation]]**
helps another reader locate the decision. Actual citations may identify a reporter,
volume and opening page or an electronic source. Our labels H1, I3 and S4 locate
paragraphs inside a fictional packet; do not present them as real reporter citations.

## Build an opinion map

Read in three passes. First, orient yourself: identify the court, date, dispute,
decision under review, and final instructions. Second, follow the reasoning slowly,
marking the legal question, decisive facts, rule and explanation. Third, compress
your understanding into a short study brief and test it against the opinion's words.
This is a reading technique, not a requirement that every court organize its writing
in the same order. A long opinion may answer several issues in separate sections.

### Heading and opening

- *Question to answer:* Which court and which dispute?
- *Note to record:* Identity and procedural setting

### Facts and history

- *Question to answer:* What happened, and what did the lower court do?
- *Note to record:* Separate event and litigation timelines

### Analysis

- *Question to answer:* What question does the court resolve, and why?
- *Note to record:* Rule, application and important qualifications

### Ending

- *Question to answer:* What happens to the challenged judgment?
- *Note to record:* Exact disposition and instructions

### Separate writing

- *Question to answer:* Who agrees with which parts?
- *Note to record:* Author and whether the reasoning commands a majority

Do not assume every sentence in the document is the deciding court speaking. An
opinion can quote a party, describe a lower court's mistake, summarize a precedent,
or present a dissent after the majority's conclusion. Write the speaker in your margin.
That small habit prevents one of the largest beginner errors: treating an argument
the court rejected as the rule the court adopted.

## The opinion and its surrounding material

A **[[syllabus]]** or editorial summary can help you orient yourself, but it is not a
substitute for the court's reasoning. The Supreme Court explains that its published
opinions are accompanied by a syllabus prepared by the Reporter of Decisions.
Read the actual opinion for the proposition you intend to use, and check the document's
own explanation of the summary's status. Commercial headnotes are also navigation
aids; do not silently attribute an editor's wording to a judge.

A **[[majority opinion]]** expresses reasoning joined by a majority of the deciding
judges. A **[[dissent]]** disagrees with the court's result; a **[[concurrence]]** agrees with
the result but may offer different or additional reasoning. Agreement with the judgment
does not automatically mean agreement with every sentence in the lead opinion.
Fragmented decisions can require more advanced analysis; this packet identifies the
joins expressly so you can practice voice attribution without guessing.

### Example 1: Map Hale before briefing it

Read H1 and H6, then H2–H5. Step one: identify the parties' roles. Hale is the borrower
who alleged an unlawful deduction; Moss is the lender who sought dismissal. Step two:
identify the lower decision. The trial court dismissed Hale's claim because it accepted
Moss's argument that actual knowledge was enough. That is background, not the appellate
court's own conclusion. Step three: locate the reviewing court's task. It asks whether
oral disclosure alone can satisfy the written-notice requirement at this pleading stage.

Step four: read the explanation in H3. Knowing terms and possessing a written record
are different things. Step five: record the ending accurately. H6 reverses dismissal
and sends the case back; it does not order Moss to repay 30 credits. Your map now tells
you what to study on the second pass. Without the map, you might write “Hale recovered
30 credits,” even though the court expressly leaves proof and repayment unresolved.

### Example 2: Keep Iman's voices separate

Read I1–I6 and ID1–ID2. First, identify the trial findings: a PDF was received, opened
before possession, and could be saved or printed. Second, mark the majority's answer:
that record satisfies the statute on these findings. Third, mark the dissent's alternative:
Judge Ortiz would require a physical document. Finally, inspect the vote line. Two judges
join the majority; the physical-paper position is a dissent, not the court's holding.

A sentence such as “Iman requires paper to protect borrowers” fails twice. It attributes
the dissent's view to the majority and omits the result. Repair it: “The Iman majority
accepted this retainable PDF; the dissent preferred a paper requirement.” Both views
are worth understanding, but they have different roles in later reasoning.

## Practice with feedback

Before continuing, make a five-line map of Sol: court; lower ruling; issue; voices;
disposition. Use S1–S6 and SC1 rather than the lesson's earlier examples. Then check:
the trial court permitted a deduction despite a sole-cause closure finding; the majority
applies section 3 independently of notice; the concurrence agrees with return of the
deduction but does not join that statutory reasoning. The appellate directions concern
20 credits, not every possible loss. If your map says only “borrower wins,” expand it
until a reader can tell what was decided and on which record.

Keep a separate list of unfamiliar words. Look up words necessary to understand the
current issue, then resume reading; do not turn every first pass into an unlimited
research project. If the opinion leaves a question open, mark it as open rather than
filling the gap from memory. That restraint will become essential during synthesis.

## Common mistakes

Highlighting nearly every line hides the structure you need. Copying a summary
without checking the opinion risks importing an editor's simplification. Reading only
the final sentence loses the explanation. Reading only the explanation loses what
the court actually ordered. Treating all judges as one voice loses the distinction
between a binding majority rationale and a separate argument.

## Key points

- Identify the court's task and ending before compressing the reasoning.
- Track the speaker of each important proposition.
- Use summaries to navigate, then verify propositions in the opinion itself.
- A study brief must preserve both reasoning and procedural result.

Source for the actual Court's document structure: [Supreme Court, Opinions](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/opinions.aspx). The worked decisions in this lesson are fictional.

lessons.title: Procedural posture, fact status and the record
lessons.body:
## The same event can support different procedural statements

You now know how to locate an opinion's parts. Next, learn why a court's account of
facts is not always a finding that those events occurred. **[[Procedural posture]]** means
the stage and setting in which the court decides an issue: for example, reviewing
a dismissal or a judgment after trial. It limits the question the court answers.
Before writing that a court “found” anything, identify what materials and assumptions
the court was permitted to use.

An **[[allegation]]** is a party's assertion. A **[[finding of fact]]** is a determination by
the relevant factfinder. A **[[stipulation]]** is an agreed proposition for the proceeding.
An **[[inference]]** is a conclusion drawn from other facts. These categories describe
different reasons a proposition appears in the opinion; they are not interchangeable.
The sentence “Hale received no writing” needs a qualifier when the opinion merely
assumes Hale's pleaded facts for a motion.

The **[[record]]** consists of the materials available for the court's decision under
the applicable procedure. Appellate courts generally review what happened below
instead of holding a new trial. That does not mean every fact question receives the
same review. Identify the particular ruling and its **[[standard of review]]**: the rule
governing how the reviewing court assesses that kind of decision. This course uses
express packet rules so that you need not invent jurisdiction-specific standards.

## Two timelines, not one

Draw the event timeline separately from the litigation timeline. In Hale, the alleged
oral disclosure, possession, late return and deduction form the first. Filing the
claim, moving to dismiss, dismissal and appeal form the second. Combining them into
one loose narrative makes it easy to treat a litigation assumption as historical proof.
For each material event, label its status and location in the opinion.

### No written notice in Hale

- *Status:* Alleged and assumed under P1
- *Safe phrasing:* Hale alleges no writing; the court assumes that for this motion

### PDF opened before possession in Iman

- *Status:* Unchallenged trial finding
- *Safe phrasing:* The trial court found timely opening; that finding is not challenged

### Desk closure solely caused Sol's delay

- *Status:* Unchallenged trial finding
- *Safe phrasing:* The appeal accepts the sole-cause finding

### An unopened email counts as delivery

- *Status:* Reserved, not decided
- *Safe phrasing:* Iman leaves that question open

These labels affect the strength of your later application. An assumed fact can be
enough to explain why a complaint survives; it is not enough to announce a final
factual victory. An expressly reserved question cannot become an answer merely
because you would prefer one side's argument.

## Read the packet's procedure before applying it

P1 tells you to accept well-pleaded factual allegations and reasonable inferences
for the borrower on the specified dismissal motion. It does not tell you to accept
every legal label. “The lender broke the Act” is a conclusion; “the clerk spoke the
terms but gave me no written record” supplies facts that can be tested against the
Act. The legal question is whether those assumed facts would establish a violation.

P2 supplies a different task after a bench trial: accept expressly unchallenged
findings and independently evaluate statutory meaning. **[[De novo review]]** is the
usual name for independent reconsideration of a legal question. It does not mean
the appeal is a new trial with new witnesses. In this packet, the factual premises
remain those supplied. Real cases require checking the applicable procedural rule,
the precise issue, and whether it was preserved; P1–P3 are teaching stipulations.

### Example 1: Fix a premature victory statement

A draft brief says, “Hale proved Moss failed to give notice, so the appeals court
awarded a refund.” Step one: compare “proved” with H1 and P1. H1 reports allegations,
not evidence resolved after trial. Replace it with “alleged.” Step two: ask what the
court decided. H4 says those allegations state a violation because oral disclosure
alone does not satisfy the statute. Step three: inspect H6. The court reverses the
dismissal and remands without ordering repayment.

The repaired statement is: “Accepting Hale's alleged absence of any written record
under P1, the appellate court held the claim legally sufficient, reversed dismissal,
and remanded for further proceedings.” This does not make the ruling trivial. It
removes the legal reason the trial court used to stop the claim, while leaving proof
for later proceedings. Precision describes the actual achievement instead of inflating it.

### Example 2: Apply P2 without retrying Sol

Suppose a reader dislikes the finding that closure solely caused Sol's delay and
suggests that Sol probably stopped for dinner. First, inspect S1: the sole-cause
finding is expressly unchallenged. Second, inspect the record: it contains no dinner
stop. Third, identify the legal issue: whether valid notice defeats section 3's
independent prohibition. The proposed dinner fact cannot be used to answer this appeal.

Now change the exercise explicitly: assume a different trial found both a borrower
delay and a lender closure contributed. That is a legitimate hypothetical, but it
is not a reinterpretation of Sol's record. Label it a new set of facts and analyze
the sole-cause requirement separately. A good reader can explore alternatives
without silently changing what the earlier court decided.

## Disposition is a procedural instruction

The **[[disposition]]** tells you what the reviewing court does with the challenged
decision. To **[[affirm]]** is to leave that decision standing; to **[[reverse]]** is to
reject it; to **[[vacate]]** is to set it aside. A **[[remand]]** sends a matter back for
further proceedings. These words can occur together, and the accompanying directions
matter. Do not infer that remand always means a completely new trial or that reversal
always awards the ultimate remedy a party requested.

Compare our cases. Hale reverses a dismissal and leaves proof open. Iman reverses
a repayment judgment with directions for judgment on the claim. Sol reverses and
directs return of a specified deduction. Each has an appellate winner, but the
instructions and remaining work differ. Keep that difference in your study brief.

## Practice with feedback

Write two sentences about Iman: one describing fact status and one describing the
legal question. A sound answer says the PDF's receipt, opening, timing and retainability
were unchallenged findings; the appellate court independently decided whether that
record satisfied the statutory notice requirement. “The appeal proved email delivery”
misstates the task. “The trial findings forced a paper requirement” confuses facts
with the legal interpretation under review.

Next, imagine only a statement that a notice was sent. List what you still need:
when it was received, whether its content could be retained, what the trial court
found, and which issue is contested. An unknown fact is a question for investigation,
not permission to assume the version that makes your preferred conclusion easier.

## Common mistakes

Avoid turning allegations into findings, importing evidence not supplied, and treating
independent legal review as unrestricted factfinding. Also avoid copying “affirmed”
without identifying what was affirmed. A precise procedural sentence often corrects
an entire mistaken brief before you reach the substantive rule.

## Key points

- Label each material proposition by its factual status.
- Identify the ruling and review standard separately.
- Read remand instructions instead of guessing the remaining proceedings.
- Keep changed-fact exercises distinct from the earlier case's record.

Background: [U.S. Courts, About the U.S. Courts of Appeals](https://www.uscourts.gov/about-federal-courts/court-role-and-structure/about-us-courts-appeals). Alder procedure is supplied fiction, not a statement of all federal or state rules.

lessons.title: Framing the issue and stating a bounded holding
lessons.body:
## Turn your map into a legal question

You can now identify a court's task and the status of its facts. The next step is to
state the **[[issue]]**: the legal question the court must answer in the setting before
it. A useful issue statement connects a rule, decisive facts and procedural context.
“Who should win?” is too broad to reveal the legal problem. “Does a blue drill count
as equipment?” is irrelevant to Hale because nobody disputes that element.

Try a three-part question: under this rule, do these material facts produce this legal
consequence at this stage? You do not need to force every sentence into an identical
template. The point is to preserve the connection between law and fact. For Hale:
under the Act's written-record condition, does a borrower state a violation by alleging
that the lender deducted a late charge after giving only oral disclosure? That question
identifies both the substantive disagreement and the limited pleading posture.

A **[[holding]]** is the court's answer necessary to decide the issue before it. Formulating
holdings can be contested, especially where a decision has several grounds or a
fragmented vote. Here, the packet deliberately identifies the issue, majority and
reserved questions. Use those signals together. The word “hold” is useful evidence,
but neither its presence nor absence relieves you from reading the reasoning and result.

## Find the right level of generality

A holding can be stated too broadly or too narrowly. “Lenders must always use paper”
overreads Hale because H4–H5 reserve electronic records. “Hale may continue this one
lawsuit involving this particular drill” underreads its legal reasoning because the
opinion explains why oral disclosure alone fails the written-record condition.
The useful middle level captures the rule the court applied and the conditions that
made it relevant without treating incidental details as legal requirements.

### Every informed borrower owes the charge

- *Problem:* Adopts Moss's rejected theory
- *Better direction:* Keep knowledge separate from the required record

### All notices must be paper

- *Problem:* Decides a reserved question
- *Better direction:* Limit Hale to oral disclosure alone

### Only Hale can use this rule

- *Problem:* Erases the stated legal principle
- *Better direction:* Describe the statutory condition, not just the name

### Hale automatically receives every requested remedy

- *Problem:* Exceeds the posture and disposition
- *Better direction:* Preserve the remand and open proof question

The best holding statement also tracks the question that matters to your later task.
For a pleading comparison, include legal sufficiency. For a medium-of-notice comparison,
highlight the absence of any written record. Neither formulation may omit a qualification
that would change the proposition being used. Keep paragraph references beside each version.

## Holding, rule, reasoning and result

The statute's condition is a **[[rule]]** supplied before the court decides the case. The
holding interprets and applies that rule to an issue. The **[[reasoning]]** explains why
the interpretation and application follow. The disposition tells what the court orders.
These parts support one another, but are not synonyms. “Reversed” is a result, not
a full legal rule; quoting section 2 is not yet an explanation of why oral knowledge
cannot satisfy it.

**[[Dicta]]** are statements not necessary to the decision of the issue before the court.
They can be thoughtful and persuasive. Calling a statement dictum does not mean it
is false or useless. It means you should not assign it the force of a holding merely
because it appears in an opinion. In difficult cases, explain why you classify a
statement that way rather than relying on a mechanical word test.

### Example 1: A worked Hale brief

First, collect the decisive facts and posture. Second, frame the issue. Third, write
the holding, reasons and disposition separately. Here is a model study brief:

Hale v. Moss Tools is a fictional Alder Court of Appeals decision in Year 1. Hale
alleged that Moss deducted a 30-credit late-return charge after providing only oral
terms and no written record. The trial court dismissed the claim because it treated
actual knowledge as sufficient. On appeal, P1 requires accepting the well-pleaded
facts for this motion, not finding them proved. The issue is whether oral disclosure
alone satisfies sections 1 and 2 so that Hale's allegations fail to state a violation.
The court holds that it does not: the Act requires a delivered written record the
borrower can retain. Actual knowledge cannot replace that condition without making
the written-record requirement ineffective. Hale therefore states a legally sufficient
claim on the assumed facts. H4 expressly leaves proof open and does not address
electronic records. H5 suggests a possible uniform paper form but does not require
one; that suggestion is not the holding. The court reverses the dismissal and remands
without ordering repayment. The brief's central limit is procedural: overcoming the
stated legal objection is not a final finding that Moss violated the Act. Relevant
pinpoints are H1–H4 for posture and reasoning, H5 for the reserved paper question,
and H6 for the disposition.

Notice what was omitted: an invented account of Hale's honesty, a general theory of
consumer protection, and damages the packet does not supply. Compression should
remove unnecessary narrative, not limitations that keep a proposition accurate.

### Example 2: Test the paper-form sentence

Take H5's suggestion that a uniform paper form might help. Ask first whether the
appeal could reach the same result without that suggestion. Yes: H3–H4 establish
that oral disclosure alone lacks the required written record. Ask next whether the
court expressly resolves paper versus electronic records. No: it expressly reserves
that question. Finally, compare the disposition: the court reverses dismissal without
ordering lenders to use a new form. These clues support treating the suggestion as
dictum rather than as a paper-only holding.

This removal test is a reading aid, not a universal formula. Some courts state alternative
grounds, and their precedential treatment can depend on jurisdiction. Do not erase
an adopted ground solely because you think the other would have sufficed. Our easy
example combines nonessential discussion with an express reservation and clear issue.

## Practice with feedback

Draft Sol's issue in one sentence, then its holding in another. A sound issue asks
whether compliant notice allows a late charge despite an unchallenged finding that
the lender's unavailable return point solely caused delay. A sound holding says that
section 3 independently bars the charge on those findings. “Closed desks always
require refunds” omits sole causation and the agreed return point. “Notice is invalid”
misstates the case: Sol's notice is compliant; a different statutory condition controls.

Then identify one question Sol leaves open. Mixed causes of delay is a good answer
because S5 expressly reserves it. Do not describe a reserved question as an implied
exception already decided. A later problem may let you reason about that boundary,
but the reasoning will be yours, supported or constrained by the earlier opinion.

## Common mistakes

Avoid writing an issue so broadly that it cannot be answered by this opinion. Avoid
using a party's requested outcome as the holding. Do not strip conditions from a
holding to make it shorter, or label all background reasoning dicta. The required
classification depends on what the court actually decided and why.

## Key points

- Frame issues with the rule, legally decisive facts and posture.
- State holdings at a useful but bounded level of generality.
- Separate holding, reasoning, disposition and reserved questions.
- Support classifications with paragraphs, not just labels.

lessons.title: Explaining reasoning and reading separate opinions fairly
lessons.body:
## Explain the bridge between rule and outcome

A correct holding is only the beginning of a useful case brief. You also need to
explain the **[[rationale]]**: the reasons connecting the rule to the outcome. If your
summary jumps from “the statute requires writing” to “the lender loses,” it leaves
out the contested step. What qualifies as writing? Which fact satisfies or fails the
condition? Why does the competing interpretation not persuade this court?

Build a reasoning chain in four parts. State the legal premise, identify the factual
premise and its status, explain the connecting inference, and state the limited
conclusion. For Hale, the statute requires a written record; the complaint alleges
only an oral conversation; oral knowledge is not a written record; therefore the
allegations describe a failure of the notice condition if proved. The final qualification
preserves the posture instead of turning the analysis into a finding after trial.

This chain also exposes missing steps. “The lender is unfair” may express a reaction,
but it does not identify the condition the lender failed. “The borrower received an
email” may identify a medium without explaining whether the content was retainable,
timely or delivered. A well-written paragraph makes the legally relevant connection
visible enough that another reader can challenge it.

## Types of reasons can work together

A **[[textual argument]]** focuses on the enacted language. A **[[structural argument]]**
reads provisions in relation to one another. A **[[policy argument]]** discusses practical
consequences or underlying goals. These are descriptions of reasoning, not automatic
rankings that decide every dispute. Ask how the court uses each argument and whether
it treats an argument as necessary, supporting, or insufficient to overcome the text.

### A conversation is not a written record

- *Function:* Connects ordinary characteristics to section 2
- *Limit:* Does not decide every digital format

### Notice cannot erase section 3

- *Function:* Reads separate conditions together
- *Limit:* Does not resolve mixed causation

### Paper might be easier to administer

- *Function:* Suggests a practical benefit
- *Limit:* Does not create a paper-only requirement

### A saved PDF contains retainable words

- *Function:* Applies statutory qualities to found facts
- *Limit:* Does not establish delivery of every sent message

The relationship between reasons matters more than counting them. Five policy
sentences do not outweigh one binding condition simply because there are more of
them. Conversely, a single word should not be detached from the provision that gives
it meaning. Explain how the opinion moves between text, facts and consequences.

## Read the losing argument in its strongest fair form

A **[[counterargument]]** is a reason supporting the competing conclusion. A **[[response]]**
explains why that reason does not defeat your conclusion, or why it changes your
confidence. Fair treatment means presenting an argument its proponent would recognize.
It does not mean pretending the competing views have identical precedential force.
Distinguish “this judge's argument deserves consideration” from “this is the rule
the court adopted.”

A separate opinion can reveal a disagreement that a quick majority summary hides.
Ask whether the judges disagree about the record, the rule's interpretation, the
application, or the remedy. In Iman, the dissent accepts receipt and retainability
but favors a physical-document requirement. In Sol, the concurrence agrees with the
repayment result but offers its own fairness rationale. Different types of agreement
and disagreement require different descriptions in your brief.

### Example 1: Reconstruct Iman without caricature

Start with the shared facts: the borrower selected the address, received and opened
the PDF before possession, and could save or print it. Next, state the majority's
legal premise: section 2 identifies qualities of a record without naming paper as
the exclusive medium. Connect those premises: this PDF has written content that
can be retained, and its delivery is established on the findings. Therefore it
satisfies the disputed notice requirement.

Now state the dissent fairly. Judge Ortiz accepts those facts but would read written
record as requiring a physical document, favoring protection for borrowers lacking
reliable electronic storage. Do not say the dissent thinks PDFs contain no words;
that is not its position. A majority-oriented response is that this borrower could
retain the delivered record and the text does not impose paper. The disagreement
is over interpretation and protection, not a factual dispute about opening the email.

Finally, distinguish legal force. The majority's bounded holding governs Alder trial
courts under P3. The dissent may help test a later argument but does not reverse
that hierarchy. A student can criticize the majority while still describing accurately
what the court decided. Evaluation and attribution are separate intellectual tasks.

### Example 2: Read Sol's concurrence without adding a rule

The vote line says Judges Vale and Lin join the majority, while Ortiz concurs in
the judgment. Step one: identify the shared result—return of 20 credits. Step two:
identify the majority's premise—section 3 bars a charge on a sole-cause finding.
Step three: inspect SC1—Ortiz proposes a general fairness explanation and expressly
does not join the statutory analysis. Step four: formulate the court's binding
proposition from the two-judge majority, not by blending all three judges' words.

A blended statement such as “Sol forbids every unfair charge” cannot be traced to
the majority. It would also erase the statute's sole-cause limitation. The corrected
brief says the majority applied section 3 on the unchallenged findings, while the
concurrence favored the same judgment for a different reason. This keeps disagreement
available for discussion without turning it into an additional enacted condition.

## Evaluate an argument without inventing support

Ask three questions of a paragraph: Is its premise supported? Does its inference
follow? Is its conclusion broader than its premises? For example, Iman's premise
supports the possibility that some electronic records qualify. It does not establish
that every emailed link qualifies. The missing facts concern content, retainability
and delivery. Marking that gap is a substantive critique, not indecision.

Be equally careful with quoted language. Record the speaker, surrounding qualification
and pinpoint. An opinion can quote a proposition to reject it in the next sentence.
A phrase removed from that setting may say the opposite of the court's reasoning.
When paraphrasing, preserve negations and conditions rather than replacing them
with a broad slogan that sounds easier to remember.

## Practice with feedback

Write a rule–fact–reason–result paragraph explaining Sol. Then write the strongest
argument for Northbank from the supplied trial ruling. Northbank relies on compliant
notice as authorization. The majority responds that notice is a necessary condition
and section 3 independently bars this deduction. A response attacking Northbank's
motives does not answer its statutory argument. A response claiming notice was absent
contradicts the record.

Now revise your paragraph so it contains one express limitation. Suitable limitations
include sole causation, the agreed return point, or the absence of a ruling on extra
damages. Compare your revised sentence with S3–S5 to see whether the qualification
matches the reason the court gave.

## Common mistakes

Do not count votes for a result as votes for every rationale. Do not make a dissent
look foolish by changing its premises. Do not treat a policy concern as a statutory
amendment. And do not confuse your criticism of an opinion with the proposition
that a lower court is permitted to disregard its holding.

## Key points

- Explain the connection between legal premise, fact and conclusion.
- Identify the exact point of disagreement between opinions.
- Address counterarguments fairly, then explain the response.
- Keep your evaluation separate from accurate attribution and authority.

lessons.title: Synthesizing a rule from several decisions
lessons.body:
## A stack of summaries is not yet a rule

You have practiced describing each opinion accurately. **[[Rule synthesis]]** is the
next step: explaining how several authorities fit together into a usable, bounded
statement. Three separate paragraphs saying “Hale won, Harbor won, Sol won” tell
a reader the results, but not which conditions explain them. Synthesis identifies
the common framework, the distinct questions each case answers, and the boundaries
that remain unsettled.

Begin with the governing text, then add what the cases actually decide. In our packet,
sections 1 and 2 concern timely delivery of a retainable written notice specifying
the charge and deadline. Section 3 imposes a separate restriction based on the cause
of delay. Section 4 supplies a limited recovery. A synthesis that discusses only the
notice medium misses part of the statute even if its summary of Hale and Iman is correct.

Before comparing facts, check authority. P3 makes these published majority holdings
binding on Alder trial courts. The packet supplies no conflicting higher authority
or later treatment. That is a stipulation for this exercise, not a general rule that
any three decisions you find online can be combined as equally authoritative. In
real research, court hierarchy, jurisdiction, date, publication status and subsequent
treatment all affect which propositions you may safely use.

## Construct a structured comparison

Make each case entry do the same work. Record posture, material facts, issue, holding and
limits. Parallel entries make differences visible; inconsistent entries can create a
false conflict by comparing one case's facts with another case's dicta.

### Hale H1–H4

- *Relevant premise:* Oral terms only, assumed under P1
- *Question resolved:* Does oral knowledge satisfy written notice?
- *Contribution to the combined rule:* Oral disclosure alone fails the notice condition

### Iman I1–I4

- *Relevant premise:* Timely delivered PDF, retainable on unchallenged findings
- *Question resolved:* Must this written record be paper?
- *Contribution to the combined rule:* This retainable PDF qualifies; Hale did not require paper

### Sol S1–S4

- *Relevant premise:* Valid notice, sole lender-caused delay
- *Question resolved:* Is valid notice enough despite section 3?
- *Contribution to the combined rule:* Notice does not eliminate the independent sole-cause bar

Read each case entry in full before comparing the same fields across cases. That ensures
you understand each holding in its own posture. Then ask which factual differences
explain the outcomes. The presence of a retainable record explains Hale versus Iman.
The independent cause-of-delay provision explains why compliant notice in Sol does
not end the analysis. No contradiction is needed to account for those results.

## Necessary conditions are not complete permission

A **[[necessary condition]]** must be present for a result to be allowed. A
**[[sufficient condition]]** is enough to produce a specified result within the relevant framework.
The phrase “only if” in section 1 makes notice necessary for the deduction. It does
not say that notice by itself makes every deduction permissible. Section 3 supplies
an additional restriction, and the description late-return charge presupposes a
late return. Keep these logical relationships visible rather than memorizing slogans.

The distinction matters whenever a learner says, “The PDF is valid, therefore the
lender wins.” Iman reaches its result on findings that also establish late return,
availability of the return point and no other asserted violation. Moving that result
into Sol while discarding those premises changes the argument. A precedent is not
a button that produces the same outcome every time one fact looks similar.

### Example 1: Build a supported synthesis

Start with the enacted conditions. Add Hale's negative boundary: oral disclosure
alone is insufficient. Add Iman's positive application: a PDF actually received,
opened before possession, and available to save or print satisfies the written-record
condition on those findings. Add Sol's independent limit: compliant notice does not
authorize a charge for delay caused solely by the lender's unavailable agreed return point.

Now write the synthesis: “Under Alder Act sections 1–3, a lender must timely deliver
a notice stating the charge and deadline in a retainable written record before it
may deduct a late-return charge. Oral knowledge alone does not satisfy that requirement
(Hale H3–H4). A delivered, retainable PDF can satisfy it on the findings in Iman
(I1–I4); a paper-only requirement does not follow from Hale. Even compliant notice
does not permit a deduction where the lender's failure to provide the agreed return
point solely caused delay (Sol S3–S4).”

Finally, attach the limits. The packet does not decide whether an unopened message
or a changing link establishes delivery and retainability. Sol does not decide all
mixed-cause disputes. Section 4 addresses recovery of the deducted portion rather
than every imaginable loss. These limits are part of a useful synthesis, not clutter
to remove when shortening it for an outline.

### Example 2: Diagnose an apparent conflict

A student writes, “Hale requires paper, but Iman permits PDFs, so the later case
overrules the earlier case.” Step one: locate the supposed paper holding. It comes
from H5's discussion of a possible form, which expressly reserves electronic records.
Step two: identify Hale's actual issue: oral disclosure without any writing. Step
three: read I2's treatment of Hale. Iman distinguishes the question it answers rather
than rejecting Hale's oral-disclosure holding. The conflict disappears once the
earlier proposition is stated accurately.

Now consider a genuinely different hypothetical: a later published opinion expressly
says oral knowledge alone is enough under the unchanged Act. You could not reconcile
that by calling an oral conversation a PDF. You would need to investigate authority,
whether an authorized court overruled the earlier holding, and whether the law or
issue changed. Do not manufacture harmony where a material contradiction remains.

## Deal with uncertainty honestly

A **[[reserved question]]** is a matter a court expressly leaves undecided. It gives
you a boundary, not an implied answer for the next dispute. A factual gap and a
legal gap also differ. Whether a borrower saved a file is a factual question. Whether
a file that cannot be saved satisfies the statute is an interpretive question. Your
memo should identify which kind of uncertainty limits the prediction.

A synthesis can be provisional. Write the strongest supported generalization, then
state what additional facts or authority could change it. Avoid claiming a broad
rule merely because no contrary case appears in a small packet. The absence of a
supplied restriction does not establish what every jurisdiction permits, especially
when the packet expressly limits its remedial and procedural coverage.

## Practice with feedback

Revise this outline entry: “Notice equals permission. Hale bans digital notice.
Sol adds an unfairness exception.” A sound revision replaces the first sentence
with notice as a necessary condition, the second with the oral-only holding, and
the third with the specific sole-cause rule. Add Iman's retainable-PDF application.
Check each proposition against a numbered paragraph rather than relying on which
case name sounds familiar.

Then write one sentence explaining why Iman and Sol produce different outcomes
despite valid notices in both. The answer should identify the cause of delay and
the independent section 3 restriction. “The judges favored different borrowers”
does not explain the rule and is unsupported by the packet.

## Common mistakes

Do not combine a majority holding with a dissent and call the mixture settled law.
Do not average inconsistent outcomes into a vague compromise. Do not confuse a
later decision's date with authority to overrule. And do not drop statutory conditions
that were undisputed in one case but decisive in another.

## Key points

- Synthesis explains relationships, not just a sequence of case summaries.
- Compare like categories and preserve each opinion's posture.
- Necessary conditions may coexist with independent restrictions.
- Identify genuine conflicts and open boundaries instead of hiding them.

lessons.title: Using analogy and distinction on a new fact pattern
lessons.body:
## Similarity matters only through a reason

Once you have a bounded rule, you can apply it to facts the earlier courts did not
decide. An **[[analogy]]** argues that legally relevant similarities support comparable
treatment. A **[[distinction]]** argues that a legally relevant difference limits that
comparison. Neither succeeds by listing surface details. Both require a bridge
between the fact and a condition or reason in the earlier case.

Suppose a new borrower rented a red camera while Iman rented a black camera. The
color difference does not affect written content, delivery, timing or retainability
on the supplied facts. Now suppose the new borrower received only a link to a page
that disappeared after five minutes. That difference could affect whether the
borrower received a written record they could retain. The second comparison identifies
a statutory reason; the first merely identifies a difference.

A **[[material fact]]** matters because it can affect the analysis under the governing
rule. Materiality is therefore question-dependent. The kind of equipment might be
irrelevant to a notice-medium issue but important under a different statute defining
covered equipment. Do not declare a fact universally irrelevant. Explain its relevance
or lack of relevance to the issue you are actually analyzing.

## Use a four-part comparison

Name the earlier holding, identify the relevant fact there, compare the new fact,
and explain why the difference or similarity matters. Finish with a prediction
bounded by the record and the authority. For example: “Like Iman's saved PDF, this
downloaded notice contains the terms in a record the borrower can retain. That
supports the section 2 condition because the majority focused on those qualities
rather than paper. Delivery and timing still require their own findings.”

### Identify authority

- *Weak version:* Iman is about email
- *Stronger version:* Iman accepts the delivered, retainable PDF on its findings

### Compare fact

- *Weak version:* Both involve computers
- *Stronger version:* Both provide a file the borrower can save before possession

### Explain relevance

- *Weak version:* They look alike
- *Stronger version:* Retention and timing address sections 1 and 2

### Bound prediction

- *Weak version:* Therefore the lender always wins
- *Stronger version:* Notice likely qualifies if delivery and the remaining conditions are established

This method is especially helpful when facts point in different directions. Rather
than counting similarities, rank them by legal significance. One decisive failure
of a required condition may matter more than ten matching background details.
The question is whether the earlier reason applies, not how many nouns match.

### Example 1: A changing link is not automatically a PDF

Consider fictional Dana, who clicks a lender's link before possession. The page
shows the charge and deadline but changes later. The supplied facts do not say
whether Dana could save or print the original content. First, identify the favorable
comparison: Dana saw written terms before taking the equipment. Second, identify
the gap: Iman relied on a record that could be retained, not merely information that
was briefly visible. Third, connect the gap to section 2.

The lender's strongest argument is that the page functioned as a written record and
could perhaps be preserved. Dana's strongest response is that viewing changeable
content does not establish possession of a retainable record. Do not decide the
missing technical fact by assuming every web page can be saved or that none can.
Ask for evidence of the delivered content, any available save or print method, and
what the trial court found about retaining the original terms.

A bounded conclusion is: “Iman supports a functional inquiry into retainable writing,
but expressly leaves changing links open. If Dana could retain the delivered terms,
the analogy strengthens; if the content could not be retained, the statutory argument
against compliance strengthens.” This is more useful than “Iman controls because
both notices are digital.” It also avoids claiming that an open question has no
reasoned answer; you can analyze it without pretending a precedent already decided it.

### Example 2: A closed desk with a different causal record

Consider fictional Leon. The lender closed the agreed desk early, as in Sol, but
Leon was still using the tool after the return deadline. The trial court expressly
finds both events caused delay. First, identify the similarity: the lender failed
to keep the agreed point available. Second, identify the difference: Sol accepted
a finding that closure was the sole cause. Third, connect that difference to the
word solely in section 3.

Leon's argument is that the closure made timely return impossible regardless of the
continued use. The lender responds that the supplied finding attributes delay to
both causes, while section 3 requires sole causation. Under P2, the reader cannot
discard the unchallenged finding to improve Leon's position. On this record, Sol's
holding does not establish the section 3 bar. That is a distinction, not a claim
that Sol was wrongly decided or no longer governs cases with its conditions.

Notice the limit: saying that this particular bar is not established does not prove
every possible deduction lawful. You must still analyze notice, late return and
any other supplied grounds. If the exercise stipulates all remaining conditions
and asserts no other violation, say so expressly when giving the narrower conclusion.

## Test one change at a time

A **[[changed-fact hypothetical]]** alters identified facts to reveal how the rule works.
Start from a clear baseline. Change one material fact or a specified group, keep
the rest fixed, and trace the consequence. If you change delivery time, notice medium,
return availability and remedy simultaneously, you may reach a different result
without knowing which change caused it.

Write independent scenarios separately. “Version A has late receipt; version B
restores timely receipt but changes causation.” Do not accidentally carry A's timing
into B. This discipline is useful beyond exams: it exposes which missing facts a
researcher or interviewer would need to investigate first.

Use **[[conditional analysis]]** when a material premise is unresolved: if fact X is
established, one argument follows; if fact Y is established, the other strengthens.
State what evidence could resolve the condition. A conditional prediction should
not be a vague “anything could happen.” It should show exactly which uncertainty
matters and how the possible answers affect the legal reasoning.

## Practice with feedback

Choose the stronger distinction from Iman: the new transaction occurred on Tuesday,
or the record arrived only after possession. Timing is stronger because section 1
requires delivery before possession. Tuesday has no supplied legal significance.
Now explain the strongest response if the lender sent the message before possession
but receipt occurred later. The response concerns the meaning of delivery; Iman
does not settle the transmission-versus-receipt boundary. Separate that interpretive
issue from the known timestamps.

Write a two-sided paragraph for Dana or Leon, then underline the sentence connecting
facts to law. If no sentence can be underlined, you have probably written a narrative
or a conclusion rather than an analysis. Add the bridge and one limitation.

## Common mistakes

Avoid similarity counting, treating every difference as material, and declaring a
distinction without naming the earlier reason it affects. Do not invent missing
evidence. Do not call a case overruled merely because it does not decide a new set
of facts. And do not let one successful analogy end analysis of independent conditions.

## Key points

- Connect every important comparison to a rule or rationale.
- Present the other side's strongest relevant comparison.
- Keep independent hypothetical changes separate.
- Tie uncertainty to specific evidence or an identified legal boundary.

lessons.title: Interpreting statutory text in context
lessons.body:
## Begin with the enacted question

Cases do not operate in a vacuum. Our three opinions interpret an enacted text,
so an application needs both the case holdings and the statute they address.
**[[Statutory interpretation]]** is the process of determining the meaning and operation
of legislation. A reader should begin by identifying the disputed words, the surrounding
provisions, any definitions, and the version of the law relevant to the problem.
Starting with a desired outcome and searching for a convenient phrase reverses that task.

Read the entire short Alder Act again. Section 1 connects delivery, content and timing
to permission to deduct. Section 2 defines notice. Section 3 adds a causal restriction.
Section 4 addresses recovery. A sentence from any one section can be accurate yet
misleading if presented as the complete framework. Your job is to explain how the
parts work together rather than selecting the provision that favors one party.

A **[[statutory definition]]** supplies a meaning for a term in the enactment. Check its
scope rather than assuming a familiar everyday meaning controls. **[[Ordinary meaning]]**
concerns how language is normally understood in the relevant context; it is not
necessarily the broadest meaning a dictionary can list. An **[[ambiguity]]** exists
when competing plausible readings remain in context, not merely whenever opposing
parties announce different preferences.

## Examine grammar, definitions and structure

Pay attention to conditions, exceptions, conjunctions and modifiers. The words only if
make timely notice a prerequisite in section 1. The word solely in section 3 limits
the causal prohibition. Removing either changes the statute. Likewise, “before the
borrower takes possession” connects the notice requirement to a specific event,
not simply to some point before the lender deducts the charge.

**[[Whole-text reasoning]]** reads a provision with the rest of the enactment. An
**[[anti-surplusage argument]]** prefers, where appropriate, a reading that gives work
to each provision rather than making words ineffective. Such interpretive principles,
often called **[[canons]]**, are tools of reasoning, not buttons that mechanically resolve
every case. Their force and interaction depend on the legal system, issue and text.
When using one, explain what words would lose their function under the competing view.

### Is a term defined?

- *Alder application:* Notice means a retainable written record
- *Error to avoid:* Replacing the definition with actual awareness

### Which modifier matters?

- *Alder application:* Solely limits the cause of delay
- *Error to avoid:* Treating any contribution as sufficient

### Do provisions operate together?

- *Alder application:* Section 3 can bar a charge despite notice
- *Error to avoid:* Treating section 1 as the whole Act

### Has the text changed?

- *Alder application:* Exercises use version 1 unless stated
- *Error to avoid:* Importing a hypothetical amendment into the baseline

Purpose and practical consequences can test readings. A retainable notice may help
people check terms later; a paper-only rule might exclude useful electronic records.
But a sensible goal does not by itself authorize rewriting an explicit condition.
State whether you are interpreting existing words or recommending a different law.
Those are distinct tasks even when the same policy concern motivates both.

### Example 1: Read the independent restriction

Northbank argues that section 1 permits its deduction because Sol received compliant
notice. First, quote or paraphrase the conditional structure accurately: a lender
may deduct only if the notice requirements are met. Second, read section 3, which
separately forbids deductions for specified lender-caused delay. Third, test Northbank's
reading against the whole text. If valid notice were always conclusive, section 3
would do no work in cases where a lender gave notice and then closed the agreed desk.

The majority's response in S3 avoids that problem by treating notice as necessary
and section 3 as an independent restriction. The facts then matter: S1 supplies an
unchallenged sole-cause finding. The conclusion follows from text, structure and
record together. It does not require a general judicial power to cancel any charge
that feels unfair. The separate concurrence's fairness argument remains a different voice.

Now imagine a hypothetical amendment deleting solely from section 3 and explicitly
applying the new text to a new transaction. The causal inquiry would change because
the legislature changed the language. You could compare Sol's reasoning, but you
could not treat its old-text holding as an answer that ignores the amendment. Conversely,
do not assume an amendment applies to an earlier event without a supplied timing rule.

### Example 2: Transfer the method to an actual opinion

Read [Taniguchi v. Kan Pacific Saipan, Ltd., 566 U.S. 560 (2012), official U.S. Reports PDF](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-566/pdf/USREPORTS-566-560.pdf).
Use printed reporter pages, which differ from the PDF viewer's page numbers.

The dispute concerned whether the federal cost category for compensation of interpreters
covered translating written documents. The majority excluded those translation costs
from that category, emphasizing ordinary meaning and statutory context. The dissent
favored a broader reading and stressed usage, court practice and access to translated
material. The Court vacated and remanded the lower decision. It did not decide that
written translation is unimportant or forbidden. See the majority at pages 564–575
and the dissent at pages 575–582.

Make two columns: majority and dissent. In each, record one textual reason and one
contextual reason with a page reference. Explain the point of disagreement before
evaluating it. This is a historical opinion-reading exercise, not a check of present
cost-recovery law. The packet quizzes remain answerable offline from the supplied
Alder materials; the external opinion is a transfer activity, not a hidden prerequisite.

## Compare plausible readings without pretending they tie

Return to Alder's delivery requirement. A lender sends a notice before possession,
but the borrower receives it afterward. A transmission reading emphasizes the
lender's completed sending act. A receipt reading emphasizes delivery to the borrower
and the opportunity to retain terms before taking possession. The statute and packet
opinions do not expressly resolve that boundary. Iman supplies facts satisfying both
timely sending and timely receipt, so its outcome cannot choose between them.

You can still assess which reading the text and reasoning better support. Explain
each premise, identify the open point, and make a qualified prediction if asked.
Do not invent an Alder electronic-transactions statute, an email-service rule, or
a court decision to make the answer more definite. Further research in a real
jurisdiction might supply such authority; this closed packet deliberately does not.

## Practice with feedback

Review this proposed synthesis: “Written record means paper because paper best
protects borrowers.” Identify the missing steps. It does not explain why the text
excludes retainable digital words, and it ignores Iman's majority holding under P3.
It resembles the dissent's view. You may present it as criticism or a proposal for
amendment, but cannot describe it as the packet's controlling notice rule.

Next, write a sentence explaining why mixed causes matter under version 1. Your
sentence should connect the finding to solely, rather than simply saying Sol looks
different. If a new hypothetical expressly changes that word, label which version
you are applying before discussing the result.

## Common mistakes

Avoid dictionary shopping for the largest conceivable meaning, reading one clause
without its definition, and using purpose to erase inconvenient words. Do not treat
a canon as universal proof. Do not confuse a historical reading exercise with verified
current authority, or a legislative proposal with law already in force.

## Key points

- Read the relevant version, definitions, conditions and neighboring provisions.
- Explain what each competing interpretation does to the text.
- Use interpretive tools as reasons, with their limits exposed.
- Distinguish interpreting current text from proposing different text.

lessons.title: Three briefs, a synthesis memo and changed facts
lessons.body:
## Put the reading skills together

The capstone asks you to produce a small portfolio, not merely select an answer.
You will brief three opinions, synthesize their rules, analyze a new record, and
test two independent changes. The objective quiz checks concepts used in that work.
It does not automatically evaluate the quality of your written legal analysis.
Use the supplied rubric for self-review or discuss the work with a qualified instructor.

Open the Alder packet, brief template, synthesis worksheet and Juno file. Read all
instructions before consulting the worked feedback below. Everything about Alder
remains fictional. No research outside the packet is necessary for this assignment,
and outside law should not be imported as if it governed Juno. The real-opinion
transfer activity in the previous lesson is separate from this closed-packet task.

## Your deliverables

Write a 200–250-word study brief for each of Hale, Iman and Sol. Include posture,
fact status, issue, bounded holding, reasoning, disposition and a useful limit.
Identify separate opinions where relevant. Use the packet's paragraph labels so
another reader can find the propositions without searching the whole document.
These are study briefs, not court filings, and the labels are not real reporter citations.

Then write a 550–750-word **[[analysis memo]]** that synthesizes the three opinions and
applies the Act to original Juno and both changed-fact versions. The total target
is 1,150–1,500 words. An **[[IRAC]]** structure—issue, rule, application, conclusion—can
help organize a paragraph. A **[[CREAC]]** structure starts with a conclusion and then
gives rule, explanation, application and conclusion. Either can work; labels alone
do not supply reasoning or correct a mistaken rule.

Allocate most of the memo to application. A reader needs to see why specific facts
satisfy or fail conditions, not just a long quotation of the statute followed by
“therefore Juno wins.” Address the strongest competing argument, state the response,
and preserve any unresolved point. Keep the two variants independent as instructed.

## Plan before drafting

First, mark the source of each premise. In original Juno, F1 establishes timely
receipt, opening and saving of the PDF; F2 identifies closure of the agreed desk;
F3 supplies the sole-cause finding and the trial court's legal rationale. Second,
identify the appellate task under P2. Third, list notice and causation separately.
Fourth, match each issue to the relevant opinion and statute before writing a conclusion.

### Notice

- *Evidence to include:* Sections 1–2; I1–I4; F1
- *Revision question:* Did I preserve delivery, timing and retainability?

### Cause of delay

- *Evidence to include:* Section 3; S1–S4; F2–F3
- *Revision question:* Did I explain why notice is not conclusive?

### Remedy and result

- *Evidence to include:* Section 4; requested relief; posture
- *Revision question:* Did I invent extra recovery or ignore appellate instructions?

### Variants

- *Evidence to include:* Each replacement fact and restored baseline
- *Revision question:* Did I accidentally combine A and B?

Write your first draft before reading the next sections. The feedback describes
reasoning a strong answer should contain; it is not a passage to copy into your
submission. You may reach a different qualified prediction on an expressly open
issue if you state the premise, acknowledge contrary reasoning and respect the record.

### Example 1: Worked feedback on original Juno

Begin with notice. Juno selected the address, received and saved the written terms
before possession, and knew the stated charge and deadline. Those findings closely
match Iman's accepted PDF. Hale does not add a paper requirement. Accordingly, the
notice objection is weak under the supplied majority holdings. State that result
without treating it as the answer to the entire case.

Next, apply section 3. Cedar closed the agreed desk before the deadline; no alternative
was agreed; the unchallenged finding identifies closure as the sole cause of delay.
Those features match Sol's material reasoning. Cedar's strongest supplied argument,
accepted below, is that valid notice authorizes the deduction. Sol answers that
notice is only one condition and does not eliminate section 3. The statutory bar
therefore applies on the original record.

Finally, connect violation to the requested relief. Juno seeks the deducted 25 credits
under section 4. The packet supports reversal of the legal ruling allowing that
deduction and recovery of the deducted portion, following Sol's approach. It supplies
no basis to add emotional-distress damages, punitive damages or attorney fees. Do
not reclassify these unchallenged trial findings as allegations on Hale's P1 motion.
Similar substantive rules can appear in different procedural settings.

### Example 2: Analyze each change independently

In version A, transmission remains at 09:00 but receipt, opening and saving occur
at 09:25, after possession at 09:20. Iman does not decide whether sending alone
establishes timely delivery. Explain the transmission and receipt readings, with
the textual and practical reasons for each. The new timing makes the notice issue
less certain; it does not require pretending the record supplies an authoritative
answer to that interpretive boundary.

Then check the rest of the file. F2 and F3 remain unchanged, so section 3 still
independently bars the deduction on the sole-cause finding. Even if Cedar wins the
delivery argument, that success does not remove the separate reason for recovery.
A good answer can identify a genuinely open issue while explaining why resolving
it is unnecessary to this particular outcome under the packet.

In version B, restore original timely receipt and saving. The new findings say
Juno's continued use after 18:00 and the closure both caused delay. Sol expressly
did not decide mixed causes, and section 3 requires sole causation. On the supplied
unchallenged finding, that condition is absent. With the original compliant notice,
late return and no other asserted statutory violation, the packet does not establish
a section 4 right to recover this deduction. Do not invent another claim or replace
the finding with your preferred causal story.

## Check your briefs before scoring the memo

Hale should preserve assumed allegations, the oral-only holding and remand without
repayment. Iman should preserve the retainable-PDF findings, the majority's medium
analysis, its limited directions and the separate dissent. Sol should preserve valid
notice, sole causation, the independent prohibition, specified recovery and the
concurrence's different rationale. If any brief fails those checks, repair it before
using it as a premise in the memo.

Now score each of the six rubric criteria from 0 to 2: posture and facts; issues and
holdings; reasoning and voice; synthesis; application; disposition and uncertainty.
The maximum is 12. This is a revision guide, not a university grading scheme or an
external pass mark. Give a paragraph reference as evidence for each 2. Revise every
0 and explain one meaningful improvement made in response to a counterargument.

## Common mistakes

Do not copy the model feedback and call it independent analysis. Do not carry version
A's late receipt into version B. Do not stop after finding notice valid. Do not turn
an open issue into a guess presented as a holding. A longer memo is not better if
it introduces facts, remedies or doctrines the assignment does not supply.

## Key points

- A complete analysis integrates accurate briefs, synthesis and application.
- Independent conditions can make one disputed issue unnecessary to the outcome.
- Keep each hypothetical's record and law explicit.
- Use the rubric to revise reasoning, not to claim automatic legal competence.

banks.title: Case Reading and Legal Reasoning questions

sections.name: Reading an opinion and procedural posture

questions.stem: What is the best first-pass question when opening Hale?
choices: Which facts will I include in a final merits judgment?
What ruling is this court reviewing and what does it order?
Which general rule can I extract before checking the court’s task?
Which party’s requested relief should I treat as the disposition?
questions.explanation: A first pass establishes the ruling under review and the court’s instructions. Preparing a final merits judgment, extracting an unbounded rule, or adopting requested relief would skip that orientation.

questions.stem: H1 describes the trial court treating actual knowledge as sufficient notice. Whose position is being described at that point?
choices: The appellate majority’s final interpretation of section 2
The lower court’s rationale, which the appeal reviews
The legislature’s binding definition of actual knowledge
Hale’s requested ruling rather than the lower court’s decision
questions.explanation: H1 describes the trial court’s actual-knowledge rationale. The appellate court reviews and rejects that theory; it is neither a statutory definition nor merely Hale’s requested ruling.

questions.stem: A prefatory summary describes a case. What should a reader do before attributing its proposition to the deciding court?
choices: Locate and check the proposition in the opinion itself
Attribute it to the court if the summary appears beside the opinion
Use it as the holding unless a dissent repeats different language
Check only that its outcome matches the final disposition
questions.explanation: Check the actual opinion’s proposition, speaker and qualifications. Placement beside an opinion and agreement about the outcome do not establish that the judges adopted the summary’s wording.

questions.stem: Which description correctly separates the voices in Iman?
choices: The majority and dissent agree the PDF fails, but disagree about relief
The majority accepts this PDF; the dissent favors a physical-document requirement
The majority accepts the PDF, and the dissent disputes its receipt
The majority requires paper, while the dissent accepts the retainable PDF
questions.explanation: I3–I4 accept this delivered, retainable PDF. ID1–ID2 accept the relevant factual findings but favor a physical-document interpretation. The disagreement is about the medium requirement, not receipt or remedy alone.

questions.stem: What does the caption alone usually fail to establish for a case reader?
choices: Which party seeks review and what ruling is under review
The names of the parties identified in that caption
The text printed in the case’s identifying heading
Whether the document includes names on opposing sides
questions.explanation: The caption identifies the case, but procedural roles and the challenged ruling need to be checked in the opinion. Do not infer them solely from name order.

questions.stem: Which note accurately records Hale’s ending?
choices: Dismissal reversed with an immediate order returning 30 credits
Dismissal affirmed, but lenders instructed to use writing in future
Judgment vacated with a finding that Moss proved valid notice
Dismissal reversed and remanded; repayment not ordered
questions.explanation: H6 reverses dismissal and remands without repayment. It neither establishes final liability nor affirms the oral-notice theory, and it does not find that Moss proved compliance.

questions.stem: How should H3 be used during the second reading pass?
choices: To trace why oral knowledge does not satisfy the written-record condition
To identify the final monetary relief ordered for Hale
To establish which factual allegations the appellate court proved
To determine the electronic-record rule expressly adopted in Hale
questions.explanation: H3 explains why oral knowledge cannot replace the required written record. It does not determine final relief, prove the pleaded facts, or adopt a rule for electronic records.

questions.stem: What are H1, I3 and S4 in this course?
choices: Labels for separately numbered statutory sections in the packet
Page references to a published Alder reporter volume
Identifiers for motions filed by the fictional parties
Paragraph labels locating material in the fictional packet
questions.explanation: H1, I3 and S4 are stable paragraph labels in invented opinions. They are not numbered statutory sections, actual reporter pages or motion identifiers.

questions.stem: Match each opinion component or judicial voice to its role.
choices: Identifies the case and parties
States what the court orders
Presents disagreement with the court’s result
Explains the connection to the outcome
questions.explanation: Caption: Identifies the case and parties; Disposition: States what the court orders; Dissent: Presents disagreement with the court’s result; Reasoning: Explains the connection to the outcome. Keep these roles distinct when reading and applying an opinion.

questions.stem: Use the lesson’s one-word label for the Reporter of Decisions’ prefatory summary: ___.
questions.explanation: A syllabus is a prefatory summary. It helps orient the reader but should not replace checking the reasoning in the opinion.

questions.stem: Under packet rule P1, how should Hale’s statement that no writing was delivered be described?
choices: An allegation assumed for the legal-sufficiency motion
A finding made after weighing the borrower’s and lender’s evidence
An agreed stipulation removing the notice issue from dispute
A legal conclusion accepted without supporting factual allegations
questions.explanation: P1 assumes well-pleaded factual allegations for the specified motion. That is different from weighing evidence, accepting an agreement between the parties, or assuming a bare legal conclusion.

questions.stem: Which statement supplies a factual allegation rather than only a legal conclusion?
choices: The lender’s conduct satisfies the legal elements of liability
The deduction violates the statutory notice requirement
Section 4 entitles me to recover the challenged deduction
The clerk stated the terms orally and gave me no written record
questions.explanation: The clerk’s actions describe events to test against the statute. Liability, illegality and entitlement to recovery are legal conclusions that need support from facts and the governing rule.

questions.stem: In Iman, the receipt and opening of the PDF are expressly unchallenged trial findings. Under P2, what is the appeal’s task on those facts?
choices: Reassess whether the borrower is credible before reaching the legal question
Accept the factual findings and defer to the trial court’s statutory meaning
Accept the findings and independently assess the statutory meaning
Treat the paper requirement as a factual finding beyond review
questions.explanation: P2 accepts the unchallenged findings while independently reviewing statutory meaning. A paper-only interpretation is a legal conclusion, not an insulated fact, and the appeal does not retry credibility.

questions.stem: A reader adds an unmentioned dinner stop to Sol’s facts. What is the problem?
choices: The reader has identified a fact the appellate court necessarily inferred
The reader has converted the concurrence’s rationale into an accepted finding
The reader has introduced evidence outside the supplied record
The reader has supplied a fact that P2 permits the appellate court to find
questions.explanation: The proposed dinner stop is outside the supplied record. Neither an inference actually drawn by the court nor a concurrence supplies it, and P2 does not authorize adding evidence on appeal.

questions.stem: What does independent, or de novo, review of a legal question mean in this packet?
choices: Reconsidering both the legal meaning and every unchallenged factual finding
Reconsidering the legal meaning without retrying the supplied facts
Accepting the trial court’s statutory reading unless it is clearly unreasonable
Reviewing only the remedy while leaving statutory meaning to the trial court
questions.explanation: Independent legal review reconsiders statutory meaning, while P2 preserves the unchallenged facts. It is not a new trial, deferential review of the legal reading, or review limited to remedy.

questions.stem: Why keep the event timeline separate from the litigation timeline?
choices: To treat events before the complaint as proved and later events as alleged
To infer that a procedural ruling resolves every earlier factual dispute
To avoid confusing alleged events with procedural assumptions and rulings
To omit the motion stage once the underlying events have been arranged
questions.explanation: Separate timelines distinguish alleged events from the motions, assumptions and rulings concerning them. Date order does not establish proof or justify omitting the procedural stage.

questions.stem: Which comparison of the three dispositions is accurate?
choices: Hale and Sol both remand without directing any repayment
Iman directs a new factual trial, while Hale directs judgment for the borrower
Hale leaves proof open, while Iman and Sol include specific judgment directions
All three reversals establish a final repayment obligation to the borrower
questions.explanation: H6 leaves proof and repayment open. I4 directs judgment for Harbor, while S4 directs return of 20 credits. A reversal does not always require either a new trial or repayment.

questions.stem: A new exercise says a court found two causes of delay. How should it be compared with Sol?
choices: As a new interpretation of the unchanged sole-cause finding in Sol
As a changed factual record, not a correction of Sol’s supplied finding
As a reason to replace the new finding with the facts from Sol
As a later legal holding that rejects Sol’s statutory interpretation
questions.explanation: The hypothetical changes the accepted record. It does not correct Sol’s existing finding, permit disregarding the new finding, or supply a later opinion overruling Sol.

questions.stem: Match each factual or issue-status label to its meaning.
choices: A party’s assertion
A factfinder’s determination
An agreed proposition
An issue left undecided
questions.explanation: Allegation: A party’s assertion; Finding of fact: A factfinder’s determination; Stipulation: An agreed proposition; Reserved question: An issue left undecided. Keep these roles distinct when reading and applying an opinion.

questions.stem: Give the lesson’s one-word procedural term for sending a matter back for further proceedings: ___.
questions.explanation: A remand sends the matter back. Its directions determine what further work remains; it does not necessarily require a complete new trial.

questions.stem: Which issue statement best fits Hale?
choices: Whether Hale proved a notice violation and established the amount owed
Whether alleged oral-only disclosure satisfies the Act’s written-notice condition on this motion
Whether oral notice may substitute for paper because no PDF was offered
Whether a failure to use a uniform form requires dismissal of a lender’s defense
questions.explanation: Hale tests whether the pleaded oral-only notice states a violation on P1’s assumptions. It does not decide final proof, require paper instead of every electronic medium, or mandate a uniform form.

questions.stem: Which proposed holding overstates Hale?
choices: Oral disclosure alone does not satisfy sections 1 and 2
Hale’s alleged absence of a written record states a violation if proved
Every compliant notice must be printed on paper
Actual knowledge does not replace the required written record
questions.explanation: H4–H5 expressly leave electronic records open. The paper-only proposition converts a nonbinding suggestion into a holding, while the other propositions track the reasoning.

questions.stem: Why is “reversed” not a complete holding statement?
choices: It identifies the winning party but also establishes every requested remedy
It gives a procedural result without identifying the legal question and answer
It supplies the applicable rule only when the lower decision followed trial
It establishes that the lower court’s factual findings were all incorrect
questions.explanation: A disposition identifies the procedural action but not the legal answer and its conditions. Reversal does not automatically award all requested relief or reject every factual finding.

questions.stem: Why is H5’s suggestion about a uniform paper form treated as dictum in the lesson?
choices: The suggestion appears after the rule analysis rather than in the opening paragraph
The suggestion concerns policy, and policy reasons cannot support a holding
The suggestion favors lenders, while the court ultimately rules for a borrower
The oral-only issue is resolved without it, and electronic records are expressly reserved
questions.explanation: H3–H4 resolve oral-only notice without H5’s form suggestion, and H5 expressly reserves electronic records. Location, policy subject matter and which party benefits do not by themselves classify a statement as dictum.

questions.stem: Which statement preserves Sol’s holding at a useful level of generality?
choices: Section 3 bars deductions whenever closure contributes to any part of a delay
Section 3 bars the deduction on the accepted finding that the unavailable agreed desk solely caused delay
Compliant notice becomes invalid whenever an agreed return point closes early
A borrower receives repayment whenever no alternative return point was agreed
questions.explanation: S3–S4 rely on the agreed return point and the accepted sole-cause finding. Closure as one contributing cause is not that condition, and section 3 does not retroactively invalidate an otherwise compliant notice.

questions.stem: What should a brief do with an expressly reserved question?
